en: The Sutra on the Fourfold Training in the Dharma,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Guṇabhadra of India during the Song Dynasty.
There are three kinds of training in virtue which are called "true training" and constitute the superior grade;
Those who maintain the training of the complete precepts are called "Inheritors of the Dharma" and constitute the middle grade;
those who receive the training of the inferior precepts are called "Relying on Merit" and constitute the lower grade;
those who practice the three matters are called "Attendants" and constitute the outer grade.
Furthermore, those who truly study the three virtues are:
first, those who are fully endowed with the practice of precepts;
second, those who possess extensive knowledge of the sutras and the Dharma.
The third is the ability to transform and deliver others.
These are the three virtues by which one is called a true scholar.

Furthermore, regarding those who receive the Dharma and observe the precepts: they purely uphold the five precepts, have faith and careful discernment regarding sin and merit, and reverently follow the teachings of the Dharma.

Furthermore, regarding those who rely on inferior precepts for the sake of merit: they observe only the first four precepts but do not observe the precept against intoxicants; they conform to worldly customs and do not change their lustful ways—this is what is meant by training based on merit.
Furthermore, there are three matters of informal service that do not constitute the precepts.
What are these three?
First, taking refuge in the Dharma with one's body.
The second is the dharma of making offerings;
the third is called the dharma of fellow students.

To maintain one's own bow and discernment, without a teacher and without anything to inherit, with a naturally inclined mind that is free from all constraints and hindrances—this is called the dharma of attending in dispersal.

The merit of true study is a hundred times superior to that of receiving the Dharma; the merit of receiving the Dharma is a hundred times superior to that of relying on blessings; the merit of relying on blessings is a hundred times superior to that of serving in a scattered manner; and the merit of such service is a hundred times superior to that of the common worldling.
Ordinary people may sometimes be inferior to animals, while animals may at times surpass humans. Why is this?
When a person commits a transgression and does not cease, they enter hell; once their punishment there is finished, they become a hungry ghost.
When their retribution as hungry ghosts is exhausted, they are reborn as animals;
when their retribution as animals is exhausted, they then return to being human.
Having fully completed their punishment among animals, they immediately attain human status.

Therefore, people should perform good deeds and uphold the teachings of the Triple Gem; they should study the Dharma of the four superior classes, thereby permanently distancing themselves from the three evil realms. Transmigrating through the heavens and subsequently being born among humans as noble and honored beings, they shall receive blessings in every lifetime, their virtue ever-increasing until they attain liberation.

In the *Sūtra on the Fourfold Training in the Dharma*, if one loses even a single aspect of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*), one should constantly train oneself according to the Dharma; when the time comes for instruction, one should attend and understand it immediately.
If one is indolent and lacks diligence, one should be moved back to a lower seat; only when later merit has been attained may one return to one's former place.
If one receives instructions but does not apply them or violates the precepts, one should be expelled and excluded from the assembly immediately, lest they corrupt others.

If there are those who have newly received the Dharma and have not yet completed three months, whatever offenses they may have committed should not be questioned at first, for they have not yet practiced it.
If all students receive and employ this Vinaya, examining one another from superiors to subordinates, they will be able to reach the ultimate goal and swiftly fulfill their great vows.
Regarding the Dharma of Attending with Scattered [Offerings], it is asked:

"If there is a son of good family who wishes to enter the Right Path and relies upon the Great Way, yet cannot endure the precepts, what practice should he perform to seek fortune and auspiciousness?"
The Master said:
"There are also three matters called the 'Dharma of Dispersed Service,' which you should joyfully uphold.
What are these three?
First, the dharmas protected by the body; second, the dharma of making offerings; third, the dharma regarding fellow practitioners.
Practicing these three matters is a hundred times superior to acting as an ordinary worldly person.
Furthermore, what is meant by the "dharma capable of attending to the person"?
Although one does not maintain the precepts, one should differ slightly from the common worldlings;

regarding places of residence and travel, one should frequently visit places where the Way of the Sūtras exists. If one encounters those who practice worldly virtues, follow their example; as for those whose conduct is evil, do not adopt it. Recognize pleasant speech and do not give names to foul words.
This is the foremost method of attending upon [the Triple Gem].
Furthermore, regarding the method of attending upon through offerings: how should one attend upon the Three Jewels?
One should never be indolent morning or evening, always turning the mind toward them, and jointly cultivate the scriptures.

If one dwells in poverty and lacks the means to make offerings, one should apply diligent effort; upon seeing others performing meritorious deeds, one should personally assist them and rejoice in their behalf in one's heart.
This is the second method of serving through dispersal.
Furthermore, what is meant by attending upon one’s fellow practitioners of the Dharma?

One should respect and love their peers without harboring arrogance; whether they sit or rise, one should keep them in mind, and whether they enter or exit, one should follow them as if observing oneself.
If they are traveling on a road, one should inquire after them when near, and wait expectantly for them from afar; take care never to turn your back on them or neglect them.
"This is the third method for providing service.
The Master said:

"Although the practitioner may not attain liberation through these three matters immediately, it is like a field with many stones and much weed; though the seeds are of poor quality, one still obtains a small harvest, which serves to sustain the time until the next planting. This is still superior to not sowing at all."
When the seeds of karma are not discarded, one will eventually encounter fertile ground; what is sown shall then flourish, and the harvest gathered shall be abundant. It is just so!
If one practices without ceasing, supported by merit and virtue, one will eventually receive the name of the True Precepts.
"Thus [he spoke]."
